title: Al-Shifa bint Abdullah
hook: who taught writing and, reports say, oversaw the market

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rufaydah, the woman of Aslam who tended the wounded by the mosque. Your line was: the tent of healing. Which nurse or carer did you thank? Day eight hundred forty-nine.

Who taught the Prophet's wife to write? The answer turns up in an unlikely place, a chapter of hadith about medicine and charms. A room in Medina. Hafsah, one of the wives of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is sitting with a woman named al-Shifa. The Prophet walks in, sees them together, and says something that only makes sense if everyone in the room already knows a small fact. Today: al-Shifa, daughter of Abdullah, and the fact the Prophet took for granted.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT HAFSAH TO WRITE?` → `TWO WOMEN IN A ROOM.` → `THE PROPHET WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: The report is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, told by al-Shifa herself. She was with Hafsah when the Prophet came in, and he said to her: won't you teach her the charm for skin sores, as you taught her writing? That's all. One sentence. But look at what it holds. Al-Shifa knew a healing recitation, the kind people said over a painful rash, and the Prophet asked her to pass it on. And in the same breath, almost in passing, he mentions that she had already taught Hafsah to write. He doesn't praise it as unusual. He uses it as the model: do this the way you did that. A woman teaching a woman to write, in the Prophet's own household, and his response is: good, now teach her this too. Her name, al-Shifa, is the Arabic word for healing, which fits the charm. But the line that lasts is the other one. She taught writing. Later reports, in biographical works compiled long after, say that the caliph Umar gave her a role in the market of Medina, keeping an eye on trade. Some scholars accept those reports, and some doubt them, and the details differ. So hold that part lightly. The part that's firm is the room with Hafsah, and a teacher whose teaching the Prophet simply assumed. There is something very ordinary about it. No speech about learning. No ceremony. Just one person who could write, sitting with one person who couldn't yet, until she could.
screen: `TEACH HER THE CHARM FOR SORES.` · `AS YOU TAUGHT HER WRITING.` · `THE MARKET: REPORTS DIFFER.` · `ONE PERSON TEACHING ONE PERSON.` · then, large: `SHE TAUGHT WRITING.`

segments.voice: The practice: teach someone to read something. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind who first taught you letters. A parent's finger under a word, a teacher, an older sibling. Breathe in, and remember the page. Breathe out, and thank them in your heart. Now look around your life for someone who could use a reader beside them. A child sounding out a sign. A parent with a confusing form. A friend learning a new script, or a new language. Choose one thing you could help them read this week. If you pray, you can ask for patience to teach well. The bell holds the time.
Al-Shifa, healing, the woman the Prophet asked to teach a charm against skin sores, as she had already taught Hafsah, his wife, to write. Today's word.
Your line: she taught writing. Today, sit beside one person and help them read one thing, slowly, all the way through. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims remember al-Shifa from a report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, where the Prophet asks her to teach Hafsah a healing charm as she had taught her writing; later biographical works add that she had a role in the market.

fork.setup: you are the Prophet. you walk in and find a woman who knows a healing charm sitting with your wife. what do you say?
options: ask her to teach your wife the charm, as she taught her writing.
fork.reveal: Abu Dawud keeps his words: won't you teach her the charm, as you taught her writing? the writing lesson was already a given.

original.note: Arabic: al-Shifa, a word meaning healing.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman remembered as a market inspector.
what it means: the firm report is that she taught Hafsah to write, and the Prophet asked her to teach a healing charm too.
what a scholar hears: Abu Dawud's one sentence pairs a charm for skin sores with writing; the market role comes from later biographical works and is debated.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 3887 (the Prophet to al-Shifa: teach Hafsah the charm for sores as you taught her writing)
Ibn Abd al-Barr, al-Isti'ab (al-Shifa and the market under Umar)

notes: The hook places the report in a chapter of hadith about medicine and charms (Abu Dawud, Kitab al-Tibb); confirm.
Abu Dawud 3887 number cited from memory; the charm is the ruqyah for namlah (skin sores/pustules). Confirm wording 'charm for skin sores'.
Market role under Umar: attributed to later reports and described as debated; confirm the source (Ibn Abd al-Barr, al-Isti'ab) and the fairness of 'some accept, some doubt'.
'Al-Shifa is the Arabic word for healing': this is the meaning of the word, not an etymology of her name; some reports say her given name was Layla. Confirm.
'A woman of Mecca and Medina' in the word segment: she was of Quraysh and emigrated; confirm.
Editor: 'read and write' cut to 'write'; Abu Dawud 3887 mentions writing only.
